I watch and listen.
I watch him through the days as he settles into his ways.
I lie awake dreaming of the one-legged man, and listen when the captain sings.
I listen to his stories.
I follow Dr. Livesey into the parlour and watch the captain as he begins his song.
I watch the captain threaten the doctor with his knife.
I watch the confrontation between the doctor and the captain.
I lay the breakfast-table, and ask the stranger who walks in what he wants.
I tell him I do not know his mate Bill, and that the table is for our captain.
I step out into the road, but hurry back in when he calls me.
I watch the stranger and the captain from behind the door.
I fetch Black Dog's rum, then retire into the bar and try to listen.
"Are you hurt?" I cry, and I run to fetch the rum.
I beg the doctor to help the captain, then fetch a basin and hold it while he opens a vein.
I help the doctor hoist the captain upstairs to his bed, and listen to his warning.
I take cooling drinks and medicines up to the captain at noon.
"I want none of your money," I say, "but what you owe my father. I'll get you one glass, and no more."
"Black Dog?" I ask.
I give him his medicine.
I watch him.
"You are at the Admiral Benbow, Black Hill Cove, my good man," I say, and hold out my hand to him.
I warn him the captain sits with a drawn cutlass, then lead him in and cry, "Here's a friend for you, Bill."
I obey the blind man and take the captain's left hand by the wrist, bringing it near to the man's right.
I tell my mother everything I know.
I go with my mother to the hamlet and tell the villagers our troubles.
I tell my mother I will go back with her, and take the loaded pistol the villagers give me.
I go down on my knees and look at the floor near his hand.
I hold Mrs. Crossley's bag while my mother counts out the captain's score from the sailor's bag.
"Mother," I say, "take the whole and let's be going."
I snatch up the oilskin packet and run out with my mother, then drag her under the little bridge when she faints.
I creep back to the bank and hide my head behind a bush of broom to watch the road.
I crouch behind the broom, listening to the chaos unfolding in the inn.
I listen to the men's voices and watch them from my hiding place.
I watch the scene unfold from my hiding place.
I watch from my hiding place as the riders trample Pew.
I leap to my feet and hail the riders.
I go back with Mr. Dance to the inn, and tell him I believe I have in my breast pocket the thing the men were after.
I ride behind Dogger to Dr. Livesey's house, knock, and ask the maid, "Is Dr. Livesey in?"
I stand and listen while Mr. Dance tells the squire and the doctor what happened.
"Here it is, sir," I say, and I give him the oilskin packet.
I eat my pie and listen to them.
I peer over the doctor's shoulder at the book.
I listen as the squire and the doctor discuss the book.
I watch as the doctor opens the seals and the map falls out.
I listen as the squire says I shall come as cabin-boy and the doctor agrees to go.
I stay at the hall under old Redruth, brooding over the map, until a letter comes and I open it.
I read the squire's letter aloud, and tell Redruth that Dr. Livesey will not like it that the squire has been talking.
I continue reading the letter.
I finish reading the letter, postscript and all.
I walk with Redruth to the Admiral Benbow, find my mother well, and take against the boy found to take my place.
I say good-bye to my mother and the cove, ride the mail with Redruth, and wake to ask, "Where are we?"
I look around at the bustling docks and the magnificent ships, feeling a sense of wonder at the sight of the sailors and the salt air.
After breakfast I carry the squire's note to the Spy-glass tavern, and watch Long John hop about on his crutch.
I walk right up to the man and hold out the note, asking, “Mr. Silver, sir?”
"Dog, sir," I say. "Has Mr. Trelawney not told you of the buccaneers? He was one of them."
"That he did, you may be sure," I say. "I knew that blind man too. His name was Pew."
I laugh along with him until the tavern rings.
I laugh along with him as we walk.
I agree with each point as Long John tells the squire and the doctor the whole story.
I watch the men as they argue.
I listen to the captain's words and watch the men.
I listen to the captain's words.
I listen to the captain's words.
I listen to the conversation and then follow them out onto the deck.
I help change the powder and the berths, and watch Long John come up the side from a shore-boat.
I am caught examining the long brass swivel amidships, and hurry off to the cook for work.
